hints: Look closely at the word starch. Remember starch is not one molecule, it is a mixture of amylose and amylopectin, so ask yourself which one is unbranched.

Recall what glycogen, amylose and amylopectin are all built from. They all use alpha-glucose joined by 1,4 and (where branched) 1,6-glycosidic bonds, so the real difference must be in branching pattern.
walkthrough:
**Recall what starch really is**

Think of starch as a team of two polysaccharides in plants. Amylose is unbranched and coiled, while amylopectin is branched.

Glycogen is the single animal storage polysaccharide, so we need a feature true for all glycogen but not true for both parts of starch.

**Compare the building blocks**

Both glycogen and starch are polymers of alpha-glucose. Both use 1,4-glycosidic bonds in the straight chains and 1,6-glycosidic bonds at branch points.

So being a polysaccharide, containing alpha-glucose, or containing 1,4 bonds cannot separate them.

**Spot the branching difference**

Every glycogen molecule is highly branched with many short side chains, even more branched than amylopectin. Amylose has no branches at all.

Therefore only the statement about all molecules being highly branched is unique to glycogen.

options.A: Correct, all glycogen molecules are highly branched, while starch contains unbranched amylose, so this clearly distinguishes them.
options.B: Both glycogen and the amylose and amylopectin in starch are polysaccharides, so this is a similarity not a difference.
options.C: Both glycogen and starch are made only from alpha-glucose monomers, so this does not distinguish them.
options.D: Both glycogen and starch have 1,4-glycosidic bonds in their main chains, so this is shared not unique.
